stories.title: From coder to orchestrator: How agents shift the role of a developer
stories.snippet: Developers are owning more of the delivery system around code, not just code itself. Join us during GitHub Universe to meet other devs, learn something new, and explore what's next. The post From coder to orchestrator: How agents shift the role of a developer appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
stories.summary: Developers are shifting from writing code to orchestrating the delivery systems around it, according to GitHub. While one-prompt demos are easy, reliable and safe code generation requires a wired workflow with checks, context, and controls. GitHub Copilot serves as a control plane, where repository events trigger GitHub Actions that invoke agents, whose output is captured in pull requests. Deterministic checks like linting, tests, security scanning, and build verification then run, while CODEOWNERS, required reviews, and branch protections govern what can merge. Agents handle ambiguous, context-heavy tasks, while developers define triggers, scope agent permissions, design handoffs, and decide where human judgment must remain. The article recommends starting small with one bounded workflow, such as issue triage or low-risk maintenance updates, and promotes GitHub Universe 2026 on October 28–29 in San Francisco.

stories.title: GitHub availability report: July 2026
stories.snippet: In July, we experienced eight incidents that resulted in degraded performance across GitHub services. The post GitHub availability report: July 2026 appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
stories.summary: GitHub experienced eight incidents in July 2026 resulting in degraded performance, including a prolonged GitHub Actions outage on August 6 caused by cascading failures in the service still running in legacy data centers. Progress toward Azure migration continued, with monolith read traffic in Azure Central US peaking at 52.75% on July 28, Git traffic reaching 47%, and 29% of repositories gaining a second replica for failover. Authentication data began migrating off the oldest shared database, with dedicated services offloading over one million queries per second at peak. Search and repository content operations moved fully to dedicated Central US infrastructure, and optimizations cut artifacts query time in half while reducing Git authorization service load by 18.2%. GitHub set targets of 70% read and 30% write traffic in Central US this quarter and a line of sight to fully exit data centers by end of 2026.

stories.title: Write your first prompt with the GitHub Copilot app
stories.snippet: Learn how to write your first prompt in the GitHub Copilot app, choose the right context and model, and start your first task with confidence. The post Write your first prompt with the GitHub Copilot app appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
stories.summary: GitHub Copilot’s first task begins with connecting an agent session to a GitHub repository or a local folder, which gives the app access to the project’s code and files. From the app’s home screen, users can select a previous project or add a new one, then describe the desired change in plain English without learning special syntax. The prompt can be refined through additional requests, since the process is iterative. Users can also choose among different AI models, keeping the default when starting out and switching when a task needs more complex reasoning or better results. The app supports voice input, lets users select an agent, and can enable remote control so sessions can be resumed from another device. Beginners should start with a small, familiar change and adjust the prompt, model, or session settings as needed.

stories.title: How to keep thinking
stories.summary: The author describes working in 2026 as frenetic, with software engineers constantly context-switching between AI agent outputs—rapidly judging answers rather than carefully reading them. They worry this shift biases their thinking toward quick skimming rather than slow, deep reflection, even though some difficult tasks like large refactors on complex codebases still require careful human thought. To preserve the habit of thinking slowly, the author recommends writing in your own words, arguing that composition itself forces you to articulate and construct ideas, whereas writing with an LLM does not. They also recommend reading dense non-fiction books, the slower the better, and have found combining both practices—reading a book and then writing about it—particularly effective. The author acknowledges that while workplaces will increasingly demand rapid switching between LLM outputs, maintaining slow thinking habits outside of work is essential to avoid losing important cognitive skills.

stories.title: No, local models will not win
stories.summary: The author argues that local AI models will not overtake datacenter inference, despite enthusiasm surrounding open-weight releases. Current frontier models are far too large to run outside GPU clusters, and as smaller models improve, users' expectations will rise accordingly—meaning the strongest affordable model will always be preferred, just as GPT-4 feels obsolete today. Datacenter models are also inherently cheaper because GPUs can batch hundreds of users' inference simultaneously for nearly the same cost as serving one, and datacenter GPUs like the B200 deliver roughly three times the flops and four times the memory bandwidth of consumer RTX 4090s. Combined, running models locally uses approximately thirty times more resources. Local models may still serve niches such as latency-sensitive voice applications, privacy-focused users, or those with unreliable internet, but these represent a small minority of overall AI usage.

stories.title: Surgical WAM: A World-Action Model for Data-Efficient Surgical Robot Learning
stories.summary: Surgical robot learning is constrained by the high cost of collecting action-labeled demonstrations, while endoscopic video is comparatively abundant. The authors introduce Surgical WAM (World-Action Model), a unified generative model built on Cosmos Policy that jointly predicts future endoscopic observations and executable surgical robot action chunks. The model is first pretrained on action-free surgical video to learn visual dynamics, then fine-tuned on a fixed budget of action-labeled trajectories, and at deployment it operates as a closed-loop, receding-horizon controller that executes a short prefix of each predicted chunk before replanning. Across four simulated surgical manipulation tasks, this video-pretraining approach improved the average success rate from 63.5% to 77.8%, including a 20 percentage-point gain on the PegTransfer task, with the largest gains observed on contact-rich and bimanual tasks. The work demonstrates that action-free video provides transferable visual dynamics priors for surgical robot control under limited action supervision.

stories.title: ConVAWG: A Retrieval-Grounded Framework for Controlled Synthetic Dialogue Generation in Violence Against Women and Girls
stories.summary: ConVAWG is a retrieval-grounded framework for generating CPS-aligned synthetic multi-turn dialogues that model Violence Against Women and Girls (VAWG) scenarios. The framework addresses the difficulty of accessing real conversation data due to privacy and legal constraints, while existing work has mostly focused on sentence-level toxicity of online abuses, leaving a gap in modeling abuse as a relational and temporally unfolding phenomenon. ConVAWG builds scenarios from persona seeds, demographic patterns reported by the UK Office for National Statistics, official crime definitions, and retrieved Domestic Homicide Review cases. It converts these into hierarchical event timelines, generates multi-scene role-play dialogues, and applies targeted activation-steered toxicity control to appropriate utterances. stories.title: Long-Horizon AI Research for Grothendieck Constant: A Case Study in Human-AI Mathematical Collaboration
stories.summary: A team of researchers presented a case study examining how artificial intelligence can be used to advance mathematical research, specifically focusing on the Grothendieck constant K_G, which measures the gap between combinatorial problems and their continuous relaxations. While the exact value of K_G remains unknown, the team tightened existing bounds to 6π/11 ≤ K_G ≤ π/(2log(1+√2)) − 10^(−4) using an AI research system that produced insights considered novel by domain experts. The paper offers a detailed account of the researchers' experience integrating AI into their mathematical workflow, including the system's demonstrated strengths and weaknesses. They also explored the conditions necessary for AI to achieve breakthrough insights in mathematics. The work falls at the intersection of artificial intelligence, computational complexity, human-computer interaction, and functional analysis.

stories.title: Test-Time Self-Evolving GUI Visual Grounding via Reflection-Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation
stories.summary: GUI Visual Grounding is a fundamental capability for GUI agents, but existing models typically freeze their parameters after deployment, limiting their ability to adapt to unseen interfaces. To overcome this limitation, the authors propose a Test-Time Self-Evolving framework that enables models to improve post-deployment without human-annotated ground truth. The framework constructs a closed-loop of Exploration, Evaluation, Reflection, and Internalization, using an MLLM-based Reflector to assess predicted grounding coordinates and provide corresponding reasoning reflections. These reflections are internalized into model weights through Reflection-Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation, which translates high-level reasoning into dense token-level supervision via a conditioned self-teacher. Additionally, a Contrastive Calibration method prevents incorrect auto-regressive prefixes from corrupting supervisory signals during failed explorations. Experiments across six benchmarks demonstrate an average accuracy improvement of 7.4% over the base model, representing the first successful exploitation of on-policy self-distillation for test-time adaptation in GUI visual grounding.

stories.title: How to Verify Consistency of Probabilistic Claims
stories.summary: The paper investigates whether a probabilistic predictor's many conditional-probability answers are self-consistent, a question motivated by AI safety concerns about honesty in AI predictions. The authors construct an interactive PCP in which a polynomial-time verifier, given circuits P (probability) and Q (confidence) specifying the model, checks approximate consistency by evaluating the circuits at few points and interacting with a single untrusted prover using a sparse witnessing distribution. They first analyze explicit probabilistic claims, placing l₂-approximate consistency of m claims of the form Pr[Y=1|X=x]=p over n Boolean variables in NP, with certificates of length O(mn + log B) where B is the input bit-precision. They further show that a small additive completeness-soundness gap eliminates the dependence on B. Together these results provide a complexity-theoretic foundation for certifying probabilistic predictors' self-consistency, viewed as a first step toward training predictive models to prove their own consistency.

stories.title: Npm-scan: Modern supply chain security for the npm ecosystem
stories.snippet: Npm-scan: Modern supply chain security for the npm ecosystem
stories.summary: npm-scan is a supply chain security tool for the npm ecosystem, distributed as the @lateos/npm-scan package and a GitHub Action under the MIT OR BLA license. It claims to detect threats that other tools like npm audit, Snyk, and Socket miss, including obfuscated payloads, credential stealers, kernel rootkits, eBPF hooks, memory extraction, GitHub spoofing, and AI-targeted attacks. The repository contains 225 commits and reports 830+ passing tests, with documentation translated into German, French, Hebrew, Japanese, and Chinese. Its structure includes dedicated api, backend, and cli directories, along with Helm deployment charts, Docker configuration, and test corpora. The project also includes validation and verification scripts, false-positive analysis files, and detection-rate benchmarks to support its production readiness.

stories.title: Show HN: Open-Source Greptile Alternative
stories.summary: Juror is an open-source GitHub tool that uses frontier AI models to review pull requests in parallel, positioned as a free alternative to Greptile. In a bundled benchmark comparing the two on a single production pull request, Juror Fast identified 4 of 6 high-severity (P0–P2) defects at 100% precision, while Greptile caught only 1 of 6 at 50% precision, though the project explicitly notes this is a manually adjudicated one-PR sample and not a statistically sufficient evaluation. The repository is MIT-licensed, requires Node 20 or higher, is distributed as a GitHub Action, and dogfoods itself by using Juror to review its own code. At the time of writing, the project had 82 stars, 9 forks, and 48 commits on its main branch.

stories.title: Tailscale Traces Database Corruption to 16y/o SQLite WAL-Reset Bug
stories.snippet: Tailscale Traces Database Corruption to 16y/o SQLite WAL-Reset Bug
stories.summary: Tailscale experienced 19 separate database corruption incidents over six months while using SQLite as their primary control plane database, a system built on shards where each tailnet's data is exclusively written by one process. The corruption affected only configuration metadata, not encryption keys or network traffic, but caused outages lasting over an hour initially as they repaired affected databases. To investigate, Tailscale engaged SQLite's developers through a professional support contract and deployed forensic telemetry, eventually building a transaction logging pipeline that revealed committed writes inexplicably disappearing without error. The root cause was traced to a bug in SQLite's Write-Ahead Logging checkpoint process, a flaw that had existed for 16 years. Recovery improvements and continuous integrity checks ultimately reduced downtime to under an hour per incident.

stories.title: DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813
stories.summary: DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 is a large-scale mixture-of-experts model from DeepSeek, representing the GA release of DeepSeek V4 Pro. The model accepts text input and produces text output, featuring a context window of 1,048,576 tokens. Pricing is set at $0.435 per million input tokens and $0.87 per million output tokens, with cache reads priced at $0.003625 per million tokens. The model was released on August 12, 2026, and is hosted exclusively by one provider through OpenRouter, which forwards every request directly without routing decisions. OpenRouter monitors the provider continuously and automatically retries on a next-best provider when errors occur.

stories.title: I hate packaging my software for Linux
stories.summary: The author struggled to distribute "Fresh" across Linux due to its fragmented ecosystem, eventually packaging it through npm, crates.io, AppImage, Flatpak, deb, rpm, AUR, nix, mise, homebrew for Linux, Terra, Gentoo GURU, and pre-built tarballs, each with drawbacks. AppImage proved unacceptably slow due to FUSE-mounted squashfs, Flatpak's sandboxing conflicted with the terminal-based tool, and official Debian/Fedora packages required maintaining all Rust dependencies. Arch's AUR is currently in read-only mode, while mise broke unexpectedly when GitHub rotated build attestation certificates. The author's plan is to make a statically linked musl binary with a built-in self-updating mechanism the primary release channel, continuing to support existing packages as alternatives.

stories.title: AI is removing the middle class of software engineering?
stories.snippet: AI is removing the middle class of software engineering?
stories.summary: AI has removed the speed limit on software production, enabling engineers to generate massive PRs and merge changes faster than anyone can review or understand them. Projects with weak engineering cultures fail faster because teams skip design discussions and prompt agents for hours, producing code that appears functional but hides accumulating complexity. Bad decisions become nearly impossible to revert because undoing migrations and deprecating structures is far costlier than creating them. Meanwhile, a single person can produce 20,000 lines of code in an afternoon, drowning reviewers in work they cannot comprehend. The author argues this widens the salary gap: engineers who can judge and architect systems become more valuable, while those who cannot are replaceable or cheaper to hire. The same dynamic is likely to play out across most knowledge work, where AI amplifies the best while making the worst almost impossible to hire.
